nameStory: The "hawkbit" name comes from an old belief that hawks would eat these plants to sharpen their eyesight - though there's no truth to this folk tale! The "autumn" part is much more accurate, as this cheerful yellow wildflower blooms much later in the season than its close relative, the common dandelion. In fact, its scientific name Scorzoneroides autumnalis literally means "autumn dandelion-like plant."
description: Autumn hawkbit is a low-growing perennial wildflower that looks remarkably like a dandelion at first glance, with bright yellow daisy-like flowers and deeply-lobed leaves growing in a flat rosette. The key difference is its branched flowering stem that carries multiple flower heads, unlike dandelions which have single flowers on unbranched stems. It typically grows 6-18 inches tall and spreads to form patches in grassy areas. This European native has quietly made itself at home across New England's lawns, fields, and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers that look like small dandelions, but here's the key - multiple flower heads on a single branched stem rather than one flower per stalk. Each flower head is about 1 inch across with numerous thin petals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, very similar to dandelion leaves but often less deeply cut. The leaves feel slightly fuzzy and have a bitter smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or patches with all leaves growing from the base - no leaves climb up the flower stems. The branching flower stalks rise 6-18 inches above the leaf rosette.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white seed heads that look exactly like dandelion "clocks" - round puffballs of seeds with feathery parachutes that blow away in the wind.

habitat: Look for autumn hawkbit in disturbed soils like lawns, roadsides, fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in somewhat poor, compacted soils and can tolerate both sunny and partially shaded locations. You'll often find it mixed in with dandelions, plantains, and other common lawn weeds in both urban and rural settings.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and form their characteristic flat rosettes, but no flowers yet - this helps distinguish it from dandelions which bloom heavily in spring.
seasonality.summer: Leaves continue growing but flowering is still rare - the plant is building energy for its late-season show.
seasonality.fall: Prime blooming time! Bright yellow flowers appear on branched stems from late summer through fall, often continuing until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Leaves may persist as withered rosettes under snow, and dried flower stems sometimes remain standing with seed heads intact.

funFact: Autumn hawkbit has a secret superpower - it can actually bloom twice in one season! If you mow or cut the first round of flowers in late summer, the plant will often send up a completely new set of blooms before winter, making it one of the most persistent wildflowers in your yard.
confusionNotes: Almost everyone mistakes this for common dandelion at first glance! The magic word to remember is "branched" - autumn hawkbit has branched flower stems with multiple blooms, while dandelions have single flowers on unbranched stems. Also remember the timing: dandelions bloom heavily in spring, while autumn hawkbit saves its show for late summer and fall.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "fall dandelion," this plant isn't actually a true dandelion at all - it just looks like one! Both plants are in the huge sunflower family and share that classic yellow composite flower structure, but they're only distant cousins. The name confusion has led many gardeners to wonder why their "dandelions" suddenly started blooming on branched stems in autumn.
compareHints: Autumn hawkbit is the only species in its genus found in New England, so your main comparison is with common dandelion and other yellow composites. Unlike dandelions, autumn hawkbit has branched flowering stems and blooms primarily in fall. It differs from hawkweeds by having all its leaves in a basal rosette rather than growing up the stem, and from cat's ear by its smoother leaves and different bloom timing.
